title: 05 — OOP, SOLID & Clean Code
html:
05 — OOP, SOLID & Clean Code

Framing: these are not style preferences. Each principle exists to reduce the cost of change in a specific, identifiable way. If you can't say which change a principle makes cheaper, you're cargo-culting it.

1. The real goal: managing change

Software cost is dominated by modification, not creation. Everything in this file optimises one metric:

When requirement R changes, how many files must I open, understand, and re-test?

flowchart LR
    A[Requirement change] --> B{How localised is the impact?}
    B -->|One class| C[Cheap: 1 file, 1 test, low risk]
    B -->|Ripple across layers| D[Expensive: N files, regression risk,<br/>merge conflicts, slow review]
    D --> E[Cause: wrong coupling,<br/>wrong module boundaries]

Two words carry the whole idea:

Term Definition Want
Coupling How much module A must know about B Low — but never zero; the goal is loose and intentional
Cohesion How related the things inside a module are High — one clear reason to exist

Types of coupling, worst to best:

  1. Content — A reaches into B's internals. (Reflection into private fields, editing another module's DB tables.)
  2. Common — shared global/mutable state.
  3. Control — A passes a flag telling B how to behave (Process(bool isRetry)).
  4. Stamp — A passes a whole object when B needs one field.
  5. Data — A passes exactly the data B needs. ✔ Target.
  6. Message — A sends an event; B may or may not exist. ✔ Loosest.

⚠️ Boolean parameters are almost always control coupling and a hidden SRP violation. Save(order, sendEmail: true) should be two methods or an explicit strategy.

2. OOP pillars — with the part that's usually skipped

2.1 Encapsulation

What: hide internal state; expose behaviour. Why: invariants can only be guaranteed if state can only change through code that enforces them.

// ❌ Anemic — every caller can violate the invariant
public class Order
{
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; set; } = new();
    public OrderStatus Status { get; set; }
    public decimal Total { get; set; }              // can drift from Lines
}
// caller: order.Status = OrderStatus.Shipped;      // shipped without payment. Nothing stops it.

// ✔ Encapsulated — invariants live with the data
public class Order
{
    private readonly List<OrderLine> _lines = [];
    public IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines => _lines;
    public OrderStatus Status { get; private set; } = OrderStatus.Draft;
    public Money Total => _lines.Aggregate(Money.Zero, (sum, l) => sum + l.LineTotal);

    public void AddLine(Product product, int quantity)
    {
        if (Status != OrderStatus.Draft)
            throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot modify an order in state {Status}.");
        if (quantity <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(quantity), "Quantity must be positive.");
        _lines.Add(new OrderLine(product.Id, quantity, product.Price));
    }

    public void MarkPaid(PaymentReference reference)
    {
        if (Status != OrderStatus.Draft)
            throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot pay an order in state {Status}.");
        if (_lines.Count == 0)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("Cannot pay an empty order.");
        Status = OrderStatus.Paid;
        PaymentReference = reference;
    }
}

The test: can any caller put this object into an invalid state? If yes, it isn't encapsulated. Note IReadOnlyList — returning List<T> hands out a mutable reference and undoes the encapsulation you just wrote.

2.2 Abstraction

Expose the what, hide the how. A good abstraction is one where the caller never needs to know the implementation to use it correctly.

⚠️ Leaky abstraction test: if IRepository<T> returns IQueryable<T>, callers must know it's EF Core (Include, deferred execution, AsNoTracking) — the abstraction leaks and provides no isolation. Either embrace EF Core directly (a perfectly good choice) or return materialised results.

Joel Spolsky's law: all non-trivial abstractions leak to some degree. The engineering judgement is how much leakage you accept for how much decoupling.

2.3 Inheritance — use sparingly

Only when: genuine is-a, stable contract, and the subclass is substitutable (§3.3). Prefer composition when: you want reuse, want to vary behaviour at runtime, or the relationship is has-a/can-do.

// ❌ Inheritance for reuse — the classic mistake
public class Rectangle { public virtual int Width { get; set; } public virtual int Height { get; set; } }
public class Square : Rectangle          // a square IS-A rectangle mathematically...
{
    public override int Width  { set { base.Width = base.Height = value; } }
    public override int Height { set { base.Width = base.Height = value; } }
}
// ...but breaks every caller that does: r.Width = 4; r.Height = 5; Assert(r.Area == 20);

// ✔ Composition
public interface IShape { double Area { get; } }
public sealed record Rectangle(double Width, double Height) : IShape { public double Area => Width * Height; }
public sealed record Square(double Side) : IShape { public double Area => Side * Side; }

Inheritance depth rule: more than 2–3 levels and behaviour becomes untraceable. Default to sealed on classes not designed for extension — it documents intent and enables devirtualisation in the JIT.

2.4 Polymorphism

Kind Mechanism Example
Subtype Virtual dispatch IPaymentProcessor.Process() with card/bank/wallet impls
Parametric Generics Repository<T>, List<T>
Ad-hoc Overloading Log(string), Log(Exception)
Structural / duck TypeScript interfaces, Python protocols interface HasId { id: string }

The core payoff: polymorphism replaces switch on type with dispatch, so adding a new type doesn't modify existing code (that's OCP, §3.2).

⚠️ When a switch is better: when the set of cases is closed and stable (order states, HTTP methods, enum-driven behaviour), a switch expression in one place is more readable than five tiny classes. C# pattern matching makes this explicit and exhaustive:

decimal fee = payment switch
{
    CardPayment c when c.IsInternational => c.Amount * 0.029m + 0.30m,
    CardPayment c                        => c.Amount * 0.019m + 0.30m,
    BankTransfer                         => 0.25m,
    WalletPayment w                      => w.Amount * 0.015m,
    _ => throw new NotSupportedException($"Unsupported payment type {payment.GetType().Name}")
};

Rule of thumb: if types change often → polymorphism. If operations change often → switch/visitor. (This is the "expression problem".)

3. SOLID — each with a real violation and its cost

3.1 S — Single Responsibility Principle

A module should have one reason to change — i.e. answer to one stakeholder/actor.

// ❌ Three actors: finance (calculation), IT (persistence), ops (reporting)
public class Employee
{
    public decimal CalculatePay() { /* finance rules */ }
    public void Save()            { /* DB schema */ }
    public string ReportHours()   { /* ops format */ }
}

Cost of the violation: a finance rule change forces recompilation/redeployment/retesting of code owned by ops and IT; merge conflicts between three teams in one file; the class needs a DB connection to unit-test a pay calculation.

// ✔ Separated by actor
public sealed record Employee(EmployeeId Id, string Name, Grade Grade, decimal BaseSalary);
public sealed class PayCalculator      { public Money Calculate(Employee e, Period p) { ... } }
public sealed class EmployeeRepository { public Task SaveAsync(Employee e, CancellationToken ct) { ... } }
public sealed class HoursReport        { public string Render(Employee e, Period p) { ... } }

⚠️ The over-application failure: SRP does not mean "one method per class". A 40-line class that does one coherent job is correct. Ask "who requests changes to this?" — if it's always the same person/team, it's one responsibility.

3.2 O — Open/Closed Principle

Open for extension, closed for modification. Add behaviour by adding code, not editing existing code.

// ❌ Every new payment method edits this method — retest everything, risk regressions
public decimal CalculateDiscount(Customer c)
{
    if (c.Type == "Regular") return 0;
    if (c.Type == "Premium") return 0.1m;
    if (c.Type == "Partner") return 0.2m;      // ← the file grows forever
    return 0;
}

// ✔ Extension without modification
public interface IDiscountPolicy
{
    bool AppliesTo(Customer customer);
    decimal DiscountFor(Customer customer, Order order);
}

public sealed class PartnerDiscount : IDiscountPolicy
{
    public bool AppliesTo(Customer c) => c.Tier == CustomerTier.Partner;
    public decimal DiscountFor(Customer c, Order o) => o.Total * 0.20m;
}

public sealed class DiscountCalculator(IEnumerable<IDiscountPolicy> policies)   // DI injects all
{
    public decimal Calculate(Customer c, Order o) =>
        policies.Where(p => p.AppliesTo(c)).Sum(p => p.DiscountFor(c, o));
}

⚠️ Don't apply OCP speculatively. Adding a strategy interface for a rule that has changed zero times in two years is over-engineering. Apply OCP at the second change, when you have evidence of a variation axis. (Rule of three.)

3.3 L — Liskov Substitution Principle

Subtypes must be usable anywhere the base type is, without the caller knowing.

The contract rules a subtype must obey:

Subtype must…
Preconditions Not strengthen them (can't demand more than the base)
Postconditions Not weaken them (must deliver at least as much)
Invariants Preserve all of the base's
Exceptions Not throw new exception types the base didn't declare
History Not allow state changes the base forbids (e.g. mutable subtype of immutable base) 
// ❌ LSP violation — strengthens a precondition
public class FileStorage       { public virtual void Save(byte[] data) { ... } }
public class S3Storage : FileStorage
{
    public override void Save(byte[] data)
    {
        if (data.Length > 5_000_000) throw new NotSupportedException();   // base allowed any size
        ...
    }
}
// Any code written against FileStorage now breaks unpredictably when handed an S3Storage.

Detection heuristics: a subclass that throws NotImplementedException; a caller doing if (x is SpecificSubtype); a subclass overriding a method to do nothing. All three mean the hierarchy is wrong — usually the base interface is too fat (→ ISP).

3.4 I — Interface Segregation Principle

No client should depend on methods it doesn't use.

// ❌ Fat interface — every implementer must implement everything
public interface IRepository<T>
{
    Task<T?> GetAsync(int id);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<T>> ListAsync();
    Task AddAsync(T entity);
    Task UpdateAsync(T entity);
    Task DeleteAsync(int id);
    Task<int> BulkImportAsync(Stream csv);   // needed by exactly one importer
}

// ✔ Segregated by client need — role interfaces
public interface IReader<T> { Task<T?> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct); }
public interface IWriter<T> { Task AddAsync(T entity, CancellationToken ct); }
public interface IBulkImporter<T> { Task<int> ImportAsync(Stream csv, CancellationToken ct); }

Practical benefit: a read-only service now depends on IReader<Order> — its unit tests need one fake method, not six; and you can see from the constructor signature that it can't write. Constructor dependencies are a design document.

3.5 D — Dependency Inversion Principle

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both depend on abstractions. Abstractions don't depend on details.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Wrong
      A1[OrderService] --> B1[SqlOrderRepository]
      B1 --> C1[(SQL Server)]
    end
    subgraph Right
      A2[OrderService] --> I["IOrderRepository<br/>(defined in the DOMAIN)"]
      B2[SqlOrderRepository] -.implements.-> I
      B2 --> C2[(SQL Server)]
    end

The critical, frequently-missed detail: the interface belongs to the consumer's layer, not the implementer's. IOrderRepository lives in the Domain project; SqlOrderRepository lives in Infrastructure and references Domain. That's what inverts the dependency — otherwise you've just added an interface without changing the direction of the arrow.

Domain (no references)  ◄──── Application ◄──── Infrastructure ◄──── API/Host (composition root)

⚠️ DIP ≠ "put an interface on everything". An interface with exactly one implementation, never mocked, never swapped, is noise. Introduce an abstraction when you need: a seam for testing, a genuine second implementation, or a layer boundary you're enforcing.

4. Other principles that carry weight

Principle Meaning Failure mode when ignored Failure mode when over-applied
DRY One authoritative representation of each piece of knowledge Fix a bug in 4 places, miss one Coupling unrelated code that merely looked alike
WET / Rule of Three Duplicate twice; extract on the third — (this is the antidote to DRY abuse)
KISS Simplest thing that works — Under-designing a genuinely complex domain
YAGNI Don't build for imagined futures — Ignoring known, dated requirements
Law of Demeter Talk to friends, not strangers: a.B().C().D() Change ripples through the chain Wrapper explosion
Tell, Don't Ask Send commands to objects rather than querying state and deciding outside Anemic model, logic scattered —
Composition over inheritance Prefer has-a Fragile base class —
Principle of Least Astonishment Behave the way the name implies GetUser() that also writes an audit row and sends email —
Fail fast Validate at the boundary, throw immediately Corrupt state discovered hours later Throwing on recoverable conditions
CQS A method either changes state or returns data, not both Hidden side effects (Pop() is a fine violation)

DRY's most important clarification: DRY is about knowledge, not characters. Two validation methods that happen to look identical today but belong to different business rules should stay separate — merging them couples two things that will diverge. The tell: when the requirement changes for one caller and you find yourself adding a boolean flag to the shared method, the extraction was wrong.

5. Clean code in practice

5.1 Naming

Guideline Bad Good
Reveal intent List<int> d; List<int> daysSinceLastLogin;
Avoid disinformation accountList (it's a HashSet) accounts
Pronounceable, searchable genymdhms generationTimestamp
No type encoding strName, IUserService on a class name, UserService
Verbs for methods, nouns for classes class Calculate class PriceCalculator, Calculate()
Consistent vocabulary fetch/get/retrieve mixed pick one
Length ∝ scope i in a 3-line loop is fine a field named i is not
Domain language data2, tempFlag settledTrades, isRebalanceRequired

The strongest test: if a method needs a comment explaining what it does, the name is wrong. Comments should explain why, never what.

5.2 Functions

  • Small. Most should fit on a screen. Not a hard rule — a linear 40-line orchestration is better than 8 one-line methods that force you to jump around.
  • One level of abstraction per function. Mixing "charge the card" with "loop over the byte buffer" in one method is the real readability killer.
  • ≤ 3 parameters. More → introduce a parameter object. Zero-or-one is ideal.
  • No output parameters (except the established TryX(out T) idiom).
  • No flag parameters (§1).
  • Guard clauses over nesting. Invert conditions and return early:
// ❌ Arrow code
public Result Process(Order? order)
{
    if (order != null)
    {
        if (order.Lines.Count > 0)
        {
            if (order.Customer.IsActive) { /* the actual work, indented 4 levels */ }
            else return Result.Fail("Inactive customer");
        }
        else return Result.Fail("Empty order");
    }
    return Result.Fail("Null order");
}

// ✔ Guard clauses — the happy path is at indent level 1 and reads top to bottom
public Result Process(Order? order)
{
    if (order is null)                 return Result.Fail("Order is required.");
    if (order.Lines.Count == 0)        return Result.Fail("Order has no lines.");
    if (!order.Customer.IsActive)      return Result.Fail("Customer is inactive.");

    // the actual work
}

5.3 Comments

Write: why a non-obvious decision was made; a link to the spec/ticket/RFC; a warning about a subtle consequence; a TODO with an owner and a ticket number; the justification for a ! null-forgiving operator or a suppressed warning. Delete: commented-out code (git remembers), redundant restatements of the code, changelogs in file headers, // end of if, auto-generated XML docs that say /// Gets or sets the Name.

// ✔ A comment that earns its place
// Fund holdings arrive T+1 but NAV is T+0, so a same-day overlap calculation
// would compare mismatched dates. We deliberately lag by one business day.
// See ADR-014 and INC-2291 (2025-11-03 incident).
var asOf = calendar.PreviousBusinessDay(today);

5.4 Error handling

// ❌ Every one of these is a production bug waiting to happen
try { ... } catch { }                                   // swallowed
try { ... } catch (Exception e) { throw e; }            // stack trace destroyed
try { ... } catch (Exception e) { _log.Error(e.Message); return null; }  // lost context, null contagion
catch (Exception) { throw new Exception("error"); }     // useless type, lost inner

// ✔
try
{
    return await _pricing.GetQuoteAsync(instrumentId, ct);
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex)
{
    // Add context the caller can act on; preserve the original as InnerException
    throw new PricingUnavailableException(
        $"Pricing service unreachable for instrument {instrumentId}.", ex);
}
// no catch-all: let unexpected exceptions bubble to the global handler, which logs
// with correlation id and returns ProblemDetails

Exceptions vs result types:

Exceptions Result<T> / discriminated union
Use for Exceptional, unexpected, unrecoverable-here Expected domain outcomes (validation failed, not found, insufficient funds)
Cost Expensive when thrown (~µs, stack capture) Free
Visibility Invisible in the signature Explicit in the signature — caller must handle
Risk Forgotten catch, control flow via exceptions Verbose plumbing; needs discipline to not .Value blindly

Guidance: exceptions for infrastructure failures and broken invariants; Result<T> for business outcomes the caller is expected to branch on. Never use exceptions for normal control flow in a hot path — a validation loop throwing 10,000 exceptions is measurably catastrophic.

5.5 Nullability

Enable nullable reference types (<Nullable>enable</Nullable>) and treat warnings as errors on new projects. Then:

  • string? means "genuinely optional" — handle it.
  • Never use ! without a comment justifying why you know better than the compiler.
  • Push null-checking to the boundary; interior code should work with non-null types.
  • Prefer Option-like patterns or empty collections over null returns. Never return null for a collection — return [].

6. Code smells → refactorings

Smell Signal Refactoring
Long method > ~40 lines, multiple abstraction levels Extract Method; Replace Temp with Query
Large class Many fields, many responsibilities Extract Class; split by actor (SRP)
Long parameter list > 3–4 params Introduce Parameter Object; Preserve Whole Object
Duplicated code Same knowledge, 3+ places Extract Method/Class; Pull Up
Feature envy Method uses another class's data more than its own Move Method
Data clumps Same 3 params travel together everywhere Extract Value Object (DateRange, Money, Address)
Primitive obsession string customerId, decimal amount everywhere Value objects with validation + typed IDs
Switch on type Repeated switch (x.Type) in many places Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
Shotgun surgery One change touches many classes Move/Inline to consolidate — cohesion too low
Divergent change One class changes for many reasons Extract Class — cohesion too low, SRP
Message chains a.B().C().D() Hide Delegate; Tell-Don't-Ask
Middle man Class only delegates Remove Middle Man
Speculative generality Abstract classes with one impl, unused hooks Collapse Hierarchy; delete it
Temporal coupling Must call Init() before Run() Constructor guarantees validity; make illegal states unrepresentable
Anemic domain model Entities are property bags; logic in services Move behaviour into entities
God object / manager OrderManager does everything Split by responsibility
Boolean trap Save(true, false, true) Named args, separate methods, or an options record

6.1 Primitive obsession — the highest-value fix

// ❌ Compiles, ships, fails in production
public Task Transfer(Guid from, Guid to, decimal amount, string currency) { ... }
Transfer(toAccount, fromAccount, 100m, "USD");     // arguments silently swapped

// ✔ The compiler now catches it
public readonly record struct AccountId(Guid Value);
public readonly record struct Money
{
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    public Currency Currency { get; }
    public Money(decimal amount, Currency currency)
    {
        if (amount < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(amount));
        Amount = amount; Currency = currency;
    }
    public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b) =>
        a.Currency == b.Currency
            ? new Money(a.Amount + b.Amount, a.Currency)
            : throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot add {a.Currency} to {b.Currency}.");
}
public Task Transfer(AccountId from, AccountId to, Money amount) { ... }

Payoff: an entire category of bug becomes a compile error; validation happens once at construction; the domain vocabulary appears in the type system. This is the cheapest big win in a typed language and it's chronically under-used.

6.2 Make illegal states unrepresentable

// ❌ 2^3 = 8 combinations, only 3 are valid
public class Shipment
{
    public bool IsShipped { get; set; }
    public DateTime? ShippedAt { get; set; }
    public string? TrackingNumber { get; set; }
}

// ✔ Only the valid states exist
public abstract record Shipment
{
    public sealed record Pending(DateTime CreatedAt) : Shipment;
    public sealed record Shipped(DateTime ShippedAt, TrackingNumber Tracking) : Shipment;
    public sealed record Delivered(DateTime ShippedAt, DateTime DeliveredAt, TrackingNumber Tracking) : Shipment;
    private Shipment() { }      // closed hierarchy
}

7. Refactoring safely

The discipline: never refactor and change behaviour in the same commit.

flowchart LR
    A[Tests green] --> B[Small structural change]
    B --> C{Tests still green?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Commit]
    C -->|No| E[Revert immediately —<br/>do not debug forward]
    D --> A

The strangler fig pattern for large-scale change: put a façade in front of the old code, route one capability at a time to the new implementation, delete old code as it goes dark. Never a big-bang rewrite — the rewrite always takes 3× the estimate and the old system keeps changing underneath you.

Characterisation tests before refactoring untested legacy: write tests that assert current behaviour (even if it's wrong), refactor, then fix the behaviour as a separate, visible change.

When NOT to refactor: code that is stable, correct, and rarely touched. Ugly code that nobody reads costs nothing. Refactor where change is happening — refactoring is an investment, and investments need a return.

8. Functional-flavoured practices that improve OO code

Practice Why C# support
Immutability by default No aliasing bugs, thread-safe for free, easy to reason about record, init, readonly struct, ImmutableArray<T>
Pure functions where possible Trivially testable, cacheable, parallelisable Static methods with no I/O
Push side effects to the edges A functional core with an imperative shell: business logic pure, I/O at the boundary —
Expressions over statements Fewer intermediate mutable variables switch expressions, ternaries, LINQ
Explicit failure in the type Caller can't ignore it Result<T>, OneOf<T1,T2>, nullable reference types
Higher-order composition Behaviour as data (policies, pipelines) Func<>, delegates, middleware

Functional core / imperative shell is the single most useful of these:

// Pure core — no I/O, no clock, no randomness. Trivial to test exhaustively.
public static class RebalanceCalculator
{
    public static IReadOnlyList<Trade> ComputeTrades(
        Portfolio current, TargetAllocation target, Money cash, DateOnly asOf) { ... }
}

// Imperative shell — all the I/O, no business rules
public sealed class RebalanceService(IPortfolioRepo repo, ITradeGateway gateway, TimeProvider clock)
{
    public async Task RunAsync(PortfolioId id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var current = await repo.LoadAsync(id, ct);
        var target  = await repo.LoadTargetAsync(id, ct);
        var trades  = RebalanceCalculator.ComputeTrades(
            current, target, current.Cash, DateOnly.FromDateTime(clock.GetUtcNow().Date));
        await gateway.SubmitAsync(trades, ct);
    }
}

Now the hard logic has zero mocks in its tests, and the shell has almost no logic to test.

9. Code review checklist

Correctness

  • Does it do what the ticket says — no more, no less?
  • Edge cases: null/empty, zero, negative, max, concurrent, duplicate, timezone/DST, rounding
  • Error paths handled; nothing swallowed; context preserved
  • Async: CancellationToken accepted and propagated; no sync-over-async; no fire-and-forget without a strategy

Design

  • Right layer? (business logic not in a controller/component)
  • Dependencies point inward; no infrastructure types in the domain
  • New abstraction justified by an actual second use or a test seam
  • Names reveal intent; domain vocabulary used consistently
  • Public API surface as small as possible (internal/private/sealed by default)

Security (detail in file 13)

  • Input validated at the boundary; parameterised SQL; output encoded
  • AuthZ checked at the right level (not only in the UI)
  • No secrets, no PII in logs

Operability

  • Structured logs at the right level with correlation; no logging in tight loops
  • Timeouts on every external call; retry only if idempotent
  • Metrics for the new path if it's on a critical route
  • Feature-flagged if risky

Tests

  • New logic has tests; bug fix has a regression test that fails without the fix
  • Tests assert behaviour, not implementation
  • No sleeps, no shared mutable state, no ordering dependence

Review manners (as a senior): separate blocking from suggestion explicitly (nit: prefix); explain the why and the cost, not just the rule; approve with comments rather than blocking on taste; if there are more than ~5 substantive comments, talk instead of typing.

10. Interview angles

  • Explain SOLID with an example of the cost of violating each. Cost, not definition — that's the senior differentiator.
  • When is inheritance the right tool? Genuine is-a with a stable contract where all subtypes are substitutable; otherwise compose.
  • What's wrong with an anemic domain model? Logic scatters into services, invariants can't be enforced, the same rule gets reimplemented inconsistently. (Counterpoint worth stating: for genuinely CRUD-shaped modules, anemic + transaction scripts is simpler and correct — DDD is not free.)
  • DRY vs coupling? DRY applies to knowledge; identical-looking code serving different rules should stay duplicated until proven to be the same rule.
  • How do you refactor a 3000-line class safely? Characterisation tests → extract cohesive clusters one at a time → each extraction its own commit → strangler façade if callers are many.
  • How do you decide something is over-engineered? Count the abstractions that have exactly one implementation and no test seam. Each one is a hypothesis about the future that hasn't paid off.
